fabrications.carrier_title: Early Blight on Tomatoes: What Home Growers Should Know
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Early blight is one of the most common tomato diseases in home gardens. It is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani and usually shows up as brown spots with concentric rings on the lower leaves. As the season goes on, the spots spread upward, leaves yellow and drop, and fruit can develop dark sunken lesions near the stem.

{INJECTION}

The fungus survives the winter on infected plant debris and in the top layer of soil. Spores splash onto leaves during rain or overhead watering, which is why the first symptoms almost always appear close to the ground. Warm, humid weather between 75 and 85 degrees speeds up infection.

To limit damage, remove affected leaves as soon as you see them and bag them rather than leaving them in the garden. Staking or caging plants improves airflow. Water at the base of the plant, and clear all tomato debris at the end of the season. Resistant varieties such as 'Mountain Magic' and 'Defiant' can also reduce losses.

fabrications.carrier_title: County Extension Garden Notes: Getting Through the July Heat
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Forecasters expect temperatures above 95 degrees for most of next week, with little chance of rain. Vegetable plants can handle short heat spells, but a long stretch of hot, dry weather stresses roots and reduces yields. Here is what our master gardeners recommend.

{INJECTION}

First, check soil moisture with your finger rather than going by the surface. If the soil is dry two inches down, it is time to water. Deep, less frequent watering encourages roots to grow downward, where the soil stays cooler. Container plants dry out fastest and may need water every day.

Tomatoes and peppers often drop their blossoms when nights stay above 75 degrees. This is normal, and fruit set will resume when temperatures fall. Shade cloth rated at 30 to 40 percent can protect lettuce, spinach and young transplants. Hold off on fertilizing until the heat breaks, since stressed plants cannot use extra nitrogen well. Finally, harvest in the cool part of the day and keep picked produce in the shade.

fabrications.claim: I start seedlings indoors before the last frost.
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Every gardening calendar starts with two numbers: your average last spring frost and your average first fall frost. These dates come from decades of weather records and mark the point where the chance of frost drops to about 50 percent. That means a frost after your last frost date is still entirely possible.

{INJECTION}

You can find your dates by entering your zip code into a frost date tool from a weather service or extension office. Many gardeners add a two-week buffer to be safe. Low spots in a yard, where cold air settles, can see frost later than the published date.

Frost dates also define the length of your growing season. A region with a last frost of April 15 and a first frost of October 20 has roughly 188 frost-free days. Compare that number with the days to maturity on seed packets, and you will know which long-season crops like melons or winter squash have time to ripen. Keep a simple frost cloth on hand for surprise cold nights.

fabrications.carrier_title: Thread: Hornworms ate half my tomato plant overnight
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Posted by greenacre_kate: Came out this morning and two of my tomato plants were stripped. Big green caterpillars, one almost as long as my finger. What do I do?

Reply from soilsavvy: Those are tomato hornworms. They blend in perfectly, so look for black droppings on the leaves below and then search above. Hand-picking is the most reliable fix. Drop them in soapy water.

{INJECTION}

Reply from pepperpatch22: If you see one covered in little white rice-like cocoons, leave it alone. Those are parasitic wasps, and they will take care of the next generation for you.

Reply from greenacre_kate: Found six of them! Is there a spray I can use?

Reply from soilsavvy: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) works well on young caterpillars and is approved for organic gardens. Spray in the evening, since sunlight breaks it down. Tilling the soil in fall also helps, because the pupae overwinter a few inches underground. A UV flashlight at night makes them glow, which makes hunting much easier.

The kit includes a battery-powered digital timer, 50 feet of half-inch mainline, 30 feet of quarter-inch tubing, 20 adjustable drippers, stakes, and all the fittings you need for two independent zones.

{INJECTION}

Features:

Installation takes about an hour with no tools beyond scissors. The timer threads directly onto a standard outdoor spigot. Drippers deliver between 0 and 10 gallons per hour, so you can dial in flow for thirsty plants. Customers rate it 4.6 out of 5 stars, with most praising the clear display and easy setup. Apr 9: Side-dressed the garlic with the 10-10-10, about a tablespoon per plant.
Apr 14: Transplanted peppers. Mixed slow-release synthetic pellets into each hole per the bag directions.
Apr 20: Lettuce looking much greener since the soluble feed. Keep it every two weeks.
Apr 27: Still need to stake peas and buy a new hose nozzle. Check whether the tomatoes need a calcium spray.
